solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Runs into Australian actor time after time escaping authority

indicators.note: whatever is escaping gets away, so those letters leave the name
going into something means ending up inside it, so one piece is placed within the other

blocks.note: the Oscar-winning actress from Melbourne
T is the abbreviation for time, twice over
R is the cricket scoring abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: Someone bursts in on a film star who keeps dodging officialdom.
explanation.walkthrough: Strip both Ts from CATE BLANCHETT and slip R in after CA. The definition hides at the end, after a surface that reads like a gossip item.
explanation.definitionFit: Carte blanche is complete freedom to act as one wishes, an unrestricted power given by someone else.

clue.text: Yellow bird

blocks.note: first meaning: cowardly, as an adjective in informal use
second meaning: the farmyard fowl

explanation.walkthrough: It looks like one phrase about a canary-coloured bird, but each word separately defines the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are informal labels for timidity, and the noun names the common domestic fowl raised for eggs.

clue.text: Such as F1 driver, one in expensive car?

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: an ace is the one in a suit of cards
RR is short for Rolls-Royce, the luxury car maker

explanation.surface: A Formula One driver sitting in a pricey motor.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface invites reading it all as one description of a driver, but 'one' gives ACE and 'expensive car' gives RR, a Rolls-Royce.
explanation.definitionFit: An F1 driver is an example of a competitor who takes part in speed contests, hence the 'Such as'.

clue.text: Comfy spot for the unchallenged prof?

definitions.text: Comfy spot for the unchallenged prof?

blocks.note: surface reading: a soft armchair to relax in
setter's reading: a professorship is a chair, and one without challenges would be an undemanding post

explanation.walkthrough: A university professor holds a chair, so an unchallenged professor's post is an undemanding one, while the phrase also names a padded armchair.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names a large upholstered armchair built for relaxing, comfortable seating for lounging.

clue.text: Tragic king‘s left lughole

blocks.note: L is the standard abbreviation for left
lughole is British slang for ear

explanation.surface: A doomed monarch has lost the hearing in one side of his head.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'has', joining definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's tragedy concerns this ancient British monarch who divides his kingdom among his daughters.

clue.text: Countrywide newspaper subject

blocks.note: first meaning: across a whole country, as an adjective
a bonus meaning: a paper sold across the whole country is called one
second meaning: a citizen of a particular state

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a single phrase about a paper's topic, but the clue gives three separate senses of the one word.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means covering a whole country; the noun is a citizen, as in a foreign citizen, or a paper with nationwide circulation.

clue.text: Wore Chinese clothing for party

indicators.note: clothing something means covering it all round, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: the Han are China's majority ethnic group
a do is an informal party

explanation.surface: Someone dressed in Chinese costume for a celebration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clothing' reads as garments but works as a verb meaning to cover. The Han are China's largest ethnic group.
explanation.definitionFit: To have a garment on is to be wearing it, so this past-tense phrasal verb equals the simple past wore.

clue.text: Dark force in America a danger to those on the street?

definitions.text: a danger to those on the street?

blocks.note: black is the darkest colour
ICE is US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, a federal agency

explanation.surface: A sinister American agency poses a threat to people on the streets.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a menacing police force; the definition is literal, about pedestrians and drivers slipping.
explanation.definitionFit: Black ice is a thin, nearly invisible glaze of frozen water on roads, a notorious hazard to motorists and pedestrians.

clue.text: Heraldic beast with very weird name

indicators.note: something weird is strange and out of normal shape, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: W is the abbreviation for with
taken as written
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: A creature on a coat of arms bears a very strange name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Weird' sits by 'name' as though describing it, but it rearranges 'very' alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A wyvern is a two-legged winged dragon used as a charge on coats of arms in heraldry.

clue.text: Convinces Santa to go round without stopping

indicators.note: the outer words go round the target, enclosing it within their letters

blocks.note: the letters run across the two words, dropping CONV at the front and A at the end

explanation.surface: Someone persuades Father Christmas to do his rounds with no breaks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go round' suggests Santa's delivery trip; here it means the two words surround the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Incessant describes something continuing without pause or interruption, an adjective matching the adverbial phrase in use.

clue.text: Rhyl Lodge, retired home for much-loved octogenarian

indicators.note: a home houses its occupant, so the letters live inside the words
to retire is to withdraw or go back, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: the letters straddling the two words

explanation.surface: A retirement home in a Welsh seaside town cares for a cherished eighty-year-old.
explanation.walkthrough: Rhyl is a seaside resort in north Wales. Dolly Parton, the much-loved country singer, turned eighty in January 2026.
explanation.definitionFit: Parton is a beloved American entertainer now in her eighties, known simply by her first name worldwide.

clue.text: After losing rear end, ricksha crashed; that’ll be the drink

indicators.note: losing its rear end means the final letter is dropped
a crashed vehicle is smashed out of shape, so the letters get jumbled

blocks.note: the word without its last letter

explanation.surface: A rickshaw wrecks its back end, and someone decides that calls for a stiff drink.
explanation.walkthrough: Ricksha is a variant spelling of rickshaw, so the A that goes is the true last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Kirsch is a clear brandy distilled from cherries, a spirit originating in Germany and Switzerland.

clue.text: My husband parked in Riviera resort road by the sea

indicators.note: a car parked in a space sits inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: Cor! is a British exclamation of surprise, like My!
the city on the French Riviera
H is the abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: Someone's husband has left the car somewhere on the Côte d'Azur seafront.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My' looks possessive but is a British exclamation of surprise. 'Riviera resort' tempts towards Monaco or Cannes; only the one that holds a husband fits.
explanation.definitionFit: A corniche is a coastal road cut along a cliff, like the famous ones above the Riviera.

clue.text: Noisily swallowed a delicious drink

indicators.note: done noisily means heard, so the sound matters rather than the spelling

blocks.note: to neck is informal British for gulping a drink down

explanation.surface: Someone gulped down a tasty drink with loud slurping.
explanation.walkthrough: In a non-rhotic British accent 'necked a' and the answer sound the same.
explanation.definitionFit: Nectar was the drink of the Greek gods, so the word is used for any especially sweet, delightful beverage.

clue.text: Sold Cava, rum, brandy

indicators.note: rum is old British slang for odd or peculiar, so the letters come out in a strange order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A drinks list: sparkling wine, rum and brandy all sold.
explanation.walkthrough: In a list of drinks 'rum' looks like another spirit; it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Calvados is an apple spirit distilled in Normandy, a type of brandy made from cider.

clue.text: Chap holding a fag back to front and beginning to imitate Tommy Cooper?

indicators.note: turned back to front means the order runs the other way
the beginning of a word is its opening letter
to hold something is to keep it inside, so one piece wraps the rest

blocks.note: a chap is a man
taken as written
fag is British slang for a cigarette, or cig
first letter

explanation.surface: A man with a cigarette, impersonating the famous comic in his fez.
explanation.walkthrough: MAN holds A, reversed CIG and I. Tommy Cooper was a British comedian famous for magic tricks that went wrong.
explanation.definitionFit: Cooper performed as a conjuror whose bungled illusions were the joke, so he is an example of the type.

clue.text: Uncomfortable, unwell, advanced torment

blocks.note: unwell means sick
A is the abbreviation for advanced, as in A level
to tease is to torment

explanation.surface: A list of symptoms: discomfort, sickness and worsening anguish.
explanation.walkthrough: The commas make it a list of woes; the first is the definition, the rest the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Being ill at ease is feeling awkward, uneasy or embarrassed, a near synonym idiom for not relaxed.

clue.text: Awkwardly sits on a hard floor

indicators.note: done awkwardly means done clumsily, so the letters end up in a jumble

blocks.note: taken as written
H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: Someone perches clumsily on a hard bare floor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Floor' looks like a noun but is the verb meaning to stun.
explanation.definitionFit: To floor someone is to surprise them so greatly they are stunned, the same as to amaze them.

clue.text: Lord moves into grand American hotel where everyone wants digs

indicators.note: when something moves it changes position, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: G is slang for a grand, a thousand
taken as written
US is the abbreviation for American
H is hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: An aristocrat checks into a smart US hotel where all the guests want lodgings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Into' sounds like insertion, but it simply joins the pieces in a row. 'Digs' means lodgings in British slang, but here it means excavations.
explanation.definitionFit: During a gold rush crowds of prospectors flock to a region, all wanting to excavate for precious metal.

clue.text: Career girl cut

blocks.note: gal is an informal word for a girl
to lop is to cut off

explanation.surface: A woman whose job has been axed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Career' reads as a profession, but here it is the verb meaning to rush headlong.
explanation.definitionFit: To career is to move swiftly and wildly, and to gallop is likewise to run or race very fast.

clue.text: Rip off coat

blocks.note: first meaning: to swindle or overcharge
second meaning: a sheep's woolly covering, or a warm jacket

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like tearing off a jacket; the phrase is the verb meaning to cheat someone.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheating people out of money is informally called this, and the noun is a sheep's wool or a soft jacket.

clue.text: Improve last opportunity when leaving DC

indicators.note: things leaving go away, so the named letters are dropped

blocks.note: the last part is the end
an opportunity is a chance
the two letters to be removed

explanation.surface: A final chance to get better as someone departs Washington.
explanation.walkthrough: DC suggests Washington, but it is just the letters D and C, taken from END and CHANCE.
explanation.definitionFit: To enhance something is to raise its quality or value, which is to make it better.

clue.text: Classic game, playing par golf going round Carnoustie finally

indicators.note: finally points to the very last letter of the word
playing with something means toying with it, so the letters are rearranged
going round something means surrounding it, so one piece encloses the other

blocks.note: taken as written
last letter

explanation.surface: A golfer shooting par around a famous Scottish course.
explanation.walkthrough: Carnoustie is a championship golf links in Scotland. Rearranged PAR GOLF wraps around E.
explanation.definitionFit: Leapfrog is a traditional children's playground pastime of vaulting over crouching players' backs.

clue.text: Foreign Office – strange place for a meeting

blocks.note: FO is the abbreviation for the British Foreign Office
rum is old British slang for odd

explanation.surface: The diplomatic ministry is an odd venue for talks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strange' looks like an anagram signal, but it supplies a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: A forum was the public square of a Roman town where people gathered, and now means any venue for discussion.

clue.text: Singular little guy, bit of a pain

blocks.note: S is the grammar abbreviation for singular
titch is British slang for a small person

explanation.surface: An odd little fellow who is rather annoying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bit of a pain' sounds like a nuisance, but it means a literal ache.
explanation.definitionFit: A stitch is a sudden sharp pain in the side, often brought on by running, so a short burst of discomfort.

clue.text: Fool to hold spades – ask for another card!

indicators.note: to hold is to grip and keep inside, so one piece goes around the other

blocks.note: a twit is a silly fool
S is the card abbreviation for spades

explanation.surface: A foolish card player clutches spades and wants to be dealt one more.
explanation.walkthrough: In pontoon, the British form of blackjack, a player says twist to be dealt an extra card.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling twist in pontoon is the request to the dealer for one more card, like hit in blackjack.

clue.text: Raise heartless army

indicators.note: without a heart means the central letter is taken out

blocks.note: to hoist is to raise

explanation.surface: Recruit a ruthless military force.
explanation.walkthrough: The I goes from the middle of HOIST. 'Raise' looks like it means to muster troops.
explanation.definitionFit: Host is an archaic word for a large body of soldiers, as in heavenly hosts.

clue.text: Old, grim smell

blocks.note: O is the abbreviation for old
dour means stern and grim

explanation.surface: A stale, unpleasant whiff.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface runs three adjectives together; only the last word is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An odour is a scent or distinctive whiff, usually unpleasant, the noun sense of the clue's last word.

clue.text: One very dead language stopped by ordinary segregation

indicators.note: a gap stopped by a plug is filled from inside, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: I is the Roman numeral one
so means very, as in so good
Latin is no longer spoken natively
O is the abbreviation for ordinary, as in O level

explanation.surface: A lone extinct tongue is cut off by everyday separation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very' as SO is a common crossword equivalence, and ordinary as O recalls the old British O level exam.
explanation.definitionFit: Segregation means keeping people or things apart, and isolation is that state of separation.

clue.text: PM Heath irate after conducting in the arena

indicators.note: conducting is directing and arranging, so the letters are put in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Prime Minister Edward Heath fumes after leading an orchestra at a concert venue.
explanation.walkthrough: Edward Heath, UK Prime Minister 1970–74, was also a keen orchestral conductor, which gives the surface its realism.
explanation.definitionFit: An amphitheatre is a round open-air venue with tiered seating around a central space, as is an arena.
